chapters.title: Complexity Analysis
chapters.description: Big-O notation and asymptotic analysis

elements.title: What is Big-O?
elements.content_inline:
What is Big-O?

Big-O notation describes the upper bound of an algorithm's growth rate as input size increases. We write O(f(n)) to say the runtime grows no faster than f(n) for large n.

Common complexity classes, from fastest to slowest:

  • O(1) — constant (hash table lookup)
  • O(log n) — logarithmic (binary search)
  • O(n) — linear (scanning an array)
  • O(n log n) — linearithmic (merge sort)
  • O(n²) — quadratic (bubble sort)
  • O(2ⁿ) — exponential (brute-force subset enumeration)

When analyzing complexity, we drop constants and lower-order terms: 3n² + 5n + 2 simplifies to O(n²).

elements.title: Analyzing Loops
elements.content_inline:
Analyzing Loops

The most common source of complexity is loops. A single loop over n items is O(n). Nested loops multiply:

for i in 0..n {       // O(n)
    for j in 0..n {   // × O(n)
        // O(1) work
    }
}
// Total: O(n²)

A loop that halves the problem each iteration (like binary search) is O(log n):

while lo < hi {
    let mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if arr[mid] < target { lo = mid + 1; }
    else { hi = mid; }
}

Recursive algorithms use the Master Theorem or recurrence relations. For example, merge sort splits in half and does linear work per level: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n).

chapters.title: Linear Data Structures
chapters.description: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues

elements.title: Array Operations
elements.content_inline:
Array Operations

Arrays store elements contiguously in memory, giving O(1) random access by index. Trade-offs:

OperationTime
Access by indexO(1)
Search (unsorted)O(n)
Insert at endO(1) amortized
Insert at positionO(n)
Delete at positionO(n)

Dynamic arrays (like Rust's Vec) grow by doubling capacity when full, giving amortized O(1) push. The key insight: even though occasional resizes cost O(n), they happen so rarely that the average cost per operation stays constant.

elements.title: Linked List Implementation
elements.content_inline:
Linked List Implementation

A linked list stores elements in nodes, each pointing to the next. Unlike arrays, insertion and deletion at a known position are O(1) — no shifting needed.

struct Node<T> {
    value: T,
    next: Option<Box<Node<T>>>,
}

Trade-offs vs arrays: no random access (O(n) to reach index k), more memory per element (pointer overhead), poor cache locality. Doubly-linked lists add a prev pointer for O(1) removal given a node reference.

In practice, arrays outperform linked lists for most workloads due to CPU cache effects. Linked lists shine when you need frequent insertion/removal in the middle and already hold a reference to the node.

elements.title: Stack & Queue Patterns
elements.content_inline:
Stack & Queue Patterns

Stack (LIFO): push and pop from the same end. Used for function call tracking, undo operations, expression parsing, and DFS.

let mut stack = Vec::new();
stack.push(1);
stack.push(2);
assert_eq!(stack.pop(), Some(2)); // last in, first out

Queue (FIFO): enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front. Used for BFS, task scheduling, and buffering.

use std::collections::VecDeque;
let mut queue = VecDeque::new();
queue.push_back(1);
queue.push_back(2);
assert_eq!(queue.pop_front(), Some(1)); // first in, first out

Both are O(1) for their core operations when implemented correctly.

elements.title: Binary Trees Explained
elements.content_inline:
Binary Trees Explained

A binary tree is a hierarchical structure where each node has at most two children (left and right). A Binary Search Tree (BST) adds an ordering invariant: left child < parent < right child.

BST operations — search, insert, delete — are O(h) where h is the tree height. A balanced BST has h = O(log n), but a degenerate tree (all nodes in one direction) degrades to O(n).

Tree traversals visit all nodes in a specific order:

  • In-order (left → root → right): gives sorted output for BSTs
  • Pre-order (root → left → right): useful for serialization
  • Post-order (left → right → root): useful for deletion
  • Level-order (BFS): visits by depth level

elements.title: Graph Representations
elements.content_inline:
Graph Representations

A graph G = (V, E) consists of vertices and edges. Two standard representations:

Adjacency Matrix: A 2D array where matrix[i][j] = 1 if an edge exists. Space: O(V²). Edge lookup: O(1). Good for dense graphs.

Adjacency List: Each vertex stores a list of its neighbors. Space: O(V + E). Iterating neighbors: O(degree). Good for sparse graphs (most real-world graphs).

// Adjacency list in Rust
let mut adj: Vec<Vec<usize>> = vec![vec![]; n];
adj[0].push(1); // edge 0 → 1
adj[1].push(0); // edge 1 → 0 (undirected)

Graphs can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, cyclic or acyclic. A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is foundational for dependency resolution and topological sorting.

elements.title: BFS vs DFS
elements.content_inline:
BFS vs DFS

Two fundamental graph traversal strategies:

Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores all neighbors at the current depth before moving deeper. Uses a queue. Guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs.

fn bfs(adj: &[Vec<usize>], start: usize) {
    let mut visited = vec![false; adj.len()];
    let mut queue = VecDeque::from([start]);
    visited[start] = true;
    while let Some(u) = queue.pop_front() {
        for &v in &adj[u] {
            if !visited[v] {
                visited[v] = true;
                queue.push_back(v);
            }
        }
    }
}

Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as far as possible along a branch before backtracking. Uses a stack (or recursion). Useful for cycle detection, topological sort, and connected components.

Both are O(V + E) for adjacency lists.

chapters.title: Sorting & Searching
chapters.description: Comparison sorts, linear-time sorts, and binary search

elements.title: Bubble Sort & Selection Sort
elements.content_inline:
Bubble Sort & Selection Sort

These are simple O(n²) comparison sorts, useful for teaching but rarely used in production.

Bubble Sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order elements. Each pass "bubbles" the largest unsorted element to its final position. Best case (already sorted): O(n) with early termination.

Selection Sort finds the minimum element in the unsorted portion and swaps it to the front. Always O(n²) comparisons regardless of input, but does at most O(n) swaps — useful when writes are expensive.

Both are in-place (no extra memory beyond a few variables). Bubble sort is stable (preserves order of equal elements); selection sort is not.

elements.title: Merge Sort & Quick Sort
elements.content_inline:
Merge Sort & Quick Sort

Merge Sort: Divide the array in half, recursively sort each half, then merge. Always O(n log n), but requires O(n) extra space for merging. Stable.

fn merge_sort(arr: &mut [i32]) {
    if arr.len() <= 1 { return; }
    let mid = arr.len() / 2;
    merge_sort(&mut arr[..mid]);
    merge_sort(&mut arr[mid..]);
    // merge the two sorted halves
}

Quick Sort: Pick a pivot, partition elements into "less than" and "greater than" groups, recurse on each. Average O(n log n), worst case O(n²) with bad pivot choices. In-place. Not stable.

In practice, quick sort is often faster than merge sort due to better cache locality, despite the worse worst-case. Most standard library sort implementations use a hybrid (like introsort or pdqsort).

chapters.title: Hash Tables
chapters.description: Hash functions, collision resolution, and applications

elements.title: Hash Functions
elements.content_inline:
Hash Functions

A hash function maps keys to array indices: index = hash(key) % capacity. A good hash function is:

  • Deterministic: same input always produces the same output
  • Uniform: distributes keys evenly across buckets
  • Fast: computable in O(1) time

Rust's HashMap uses SipHash by default (resistant to hash-flooding DoS attacks). For cryptographic use, you'd use SHA-256 or BLAKE3 — much slower but collision-resistant.

The load factor α = n/m (items / capacity) determines performance. Most implementations resize when α exceeds ~0.75.

elements.title: Collision Resolution
elements.content_inline:
Collision Resolution

When two keys hash to the same index, we have a collision. Two main strategies:

Chaining: Each bucket holds a linked list (or vec) of entries. Simple, degrades gracefully — worst case O(n) if all keys collide, but average O(1 + α).

Open Addressing: Store all entries in the array itself. On collision, probe for the next empty slot:

  • Linear probing: check index+1, index+2, … (cache-friendly but causes clustering)
  • Quadratic probing: check index+1², index+2², … (reduces clustering)
  • Double hashing: use a second hash function for step size

Robin Hood hashing (used in Rust's hashbrown) is a variant of linear probing that moves existing entries to reduce variance in probe lengths.

elements.title: Semantic HTML
elements.content_inline:
Semantic HTML

Semantic elements describe their content's meaning, not just appearance. Using <article>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <header>, and <footer> improves accessibility, SEO, and code readability.

Common anti-patterns: using <div> for everything, using <table> for layout, skipping heading levels. Screen readers rely on semantic structure to navigate the page.

Key rule: choose the element that best describes the content's purpose, not its visual appearance. Use CSS for styling.

elements.title: Flexbox & Grid
elements.content_inline:
Flexbox & Grid

Flexbox is for one-dimensional layouts (row or column). Set display: flex on the container, then control alignment with justify-content, align-items, and gap.

.container {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
  justify-content: space-between;
}

CSS Grid is for two-dimensional layouts. Define rows and columns explicitly:

.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 1rem;
}

Rule of thumb: use Flexbox for component-level layout, Grid for page-level layout. They compose well together.

elements.title: CSS Layout Workshop
elements.content_inline:
CSS Layout Workshop

Practice building responsive layouts using Flexbox and CSS Grid in this hands-on workshop.

Exercise 1: Flexbox Navigation Bar

Create a horizontal navigation bar with the logo on the left and links on the right:

/* Your goal: */
.navbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center;
  padding: 1rem 2rem;
}

.nav-links {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

Exercise 2: Grid Product Cards

Build a responsive card grid that shows 1 column on mobile, 2 on tablet, 3 on desktop:

.card-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(280px, 1fr));
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

Exercise 3: Holy Grail Layout

Combine Grid and Flexbox to build the classic "holy grail" layout: header, footer, main content area with two sidebars. The main content should be fluid, sidebars fixed-width.

elements.title: ES6+ Features
elements.content_inline:
ES6+ Features

Modern JavaScript (ES6/ES2015+) introduced features that are now standard:

  • let/const — block-scoped variables (prefer const)
  • Arrow functions: const add = (a, b) => a + b
  • Template literals: `Hello ${name}`
  • Destructuring: const { x, y } = point
  • Spread/rest: [...arr], { ...obj }
  • Modules: import/export
  • Optional chaining: user?.address?.city
  • Nullish coalescing: value ?? 'default'

These features make code more concise and expressive. TypeScript builds on top of ES6+ by adding a static type system.

elements.title: Async/Await Patterns
elements.content_inline:
Async/Await Patterns

JavaScript is single-threaded but non-blocking, using an event loop for I/O. async/await provides clean syntax over Promises:

async function fetchUser(id) {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

Key patterns:

  • Parallel: await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()])
  • Sequential: const a = await fetchA(); const b = await fetchB(a.id);
  • Error handling: wrap in try/catch, or use .catch()

Avoid: await inside loops when the iterations are independent (use Promise.all with .map() instead).

elements.title: TypeScript Type System
elements.content_inline:
TypeScript Type System

TypeScript adds compile-time type checking to JavaScript. Core concepts:

// Interfaces define object shapes
interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email?: string; // optional
}

// Generics for reusable types
type Result<T> = { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: string };

// Union and literal types
type Status = 'active' | 'inactive' | 'pending';

// Type guards narrow types at runtime
function isUser(x: unknown): x is User {
  return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'id' in x;
}

TypeScript's type system is structural (duck typing), not nominal. Two types with the same shape are compatible regardless of name. Use strict: true in tsconfig.json for maximum safety.

chapters.title: Vue 3 & Composition API
chapters.description: Reactivity, composables, routing, and state management

elements.title: Vue Reactivity System
elements.content_inline:
Vue Reactivity System

Vue 3's reactivity is built on JavaScript Proxies. When you create a ref() or reactive(), Vue wraps the value and tracks which components read it. When the value changes, only those components re-render.

import { ref, computed, watch } from 'vue';

const count = ref(0);
const doubled = computed(() => count.value * 2);

watch(count, (newVal, oldVal) => {
  console.log(`changed from ${oldVal} to ${newVal}`);
});

count.value++; // triggers computed + watcher

ref() wraps primitives (access via .value). reactive() wraps objects (direct property access). In templates, .value is auto-unwrapped.

elements.title: Composables Pattern
elements.content_inline:
Composables Pattern

Composables are functions that encapsulate reactive state and logic, following the naming convention use*. They're Vue's answer to React hooks:

// composables/useCounter.ts
export function useCounter(initial = 0) {
  const count = ref(initial);
  const increment = () => count.value++;
  const decrement = () => count.value--;
  const reset = () => count.value = initial;
  return { count, increment, decrement, reset };
}

Composables can use other composables, lifecycle hooks, and watchers. They promote code reuse without mixins or inheritance. Each call creates independent state.

Best practices: return refs (not raw values) so consumers retain reactivity, keep composables focused on one concern, and handle cleanup in onUnmounted.

elements.title: Building REST APIs in Rust
elements.content_inline:
Building REST APIs in Rust

Rust's type system and performance make it excellent for backend APIs. Common frameworks: Actix Web, Axum, Rocket. A minimal Axum handler:

use axum::{Json, extract::Path};

async fn get_user(Path(id): Path<String>) -> Json<User> {
    let user = db::find_user(&id).await.unwrap();
    Json(user)
}

Key Rust backend patterns:

  • Extractors: parse request parts (path, query, body) into typed values
  • Middleware: logging, auth, CORS via tower layers
  • Error handling: implement IntoResponse for custom error types
  • Shared state: Arc<AppState> passed via extension

elements.title: Database Design & Migrations
elements.content_inline:
Database Design & Migrations

Good schema design starts with identifying entities and relationships. Key principles:

  • Normalization: eliminate redundancy (3NF is usually sufficient)
  • Foreign keys: enforce referential integrity
  • Indexes: add on columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY
  • Migrations: version-controlled schema changes (never edit production directly)
CREATE TABLE users (
    id    TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name  TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);

For embedded apps, SQLite is ideal: zero configuration, single-file database, excellent read performance with WAL mode.

elements.title: Authentication with JWT
elements.content_inline:
Authentication with JWT

JSON Web Tokens (JWT) encode claims as a signed JSON payload. The flow:

  1. User submits credentials (username + password)
  2. Server verifies, creates a JWT with user ID and expiry
  3. Client stores the token and sends it in Authorization: Bearer <token>
  4. Server validates the signature on each request

A JWT has three parts: header.payload.signature (base64url-encoded). The signature ensures the token hasn't been tampered with.

Security considerations: keep tokens short-lived (15-60 min), use refresh tokens for re-authentication, never store JWTs in localStorage (use httpOnly cookies), and always validate the exp claim server-side.

elements.title: Linear Regression from Scratch
elements.content_inline:
Linear Regression from Scratch

Linear regression models the relationship y = wx + b by finding weights w and bias b that minimize the mean squared error (MSE):

MSE = (1/n) Σ (yᵢ - (wxᵢ + b))²

Gradient descent iteratively updates parameters in the direction that reduces error:

w = w - lr * ∂MSE/∂w
b = b - lr * ∂MSE/∂b

The learning rate lr controls step size. Too large: overshooting. Too small: slow convergence. For multiple features, w becomes a vector and the model is y = Xw + b (solvable analytically via the normal equation).

elements.title: Logistic Regression
elements.content_inline:
Logistic Regression

Despite its name, logistic regression is a classification algorithm. It predicts the probability that an input belongs to class 1:

P(y=1|x) = σ(wx + b) = 1 / (1 + e^(-(wx + b)))

The sigmoid function σ squashes any real number to [0, 1]. We use binary cross-entropy as the loss function (not MSE), which is convex and works well with gradient descent.

Decision boundary: predict class 1 if P ≥ 0.5, class 0 otherwise. The threshold can be tuned depending on whether false positives or false negatives are more costly.

chapters.title: Classification & Clustering
chapters.description: SVMs, decision trees, k-means, and DBSCAN

elements.title: Decision Trees & Random Forests
elements.content_inline:
Decision Trees & Random Forests

A decision tree splits data by asking yes/no questions about features, choosing splits that maximize information gain (or minimize Gini impurity). Easy to interpret but prone to overfitting.

Random Forests fix overfitting by training many trees on random subsets of data and features, then averaging their predictions (bagging). Key hyperparameters:

  • n_estimators: number of trees (more = better, diminishing returns)
  • max_depth: limits tree depth to prevent overfitting
  • max_features: number of features considered per split (typically √p)

Random forests are a strong baseline for tabular data — fast to train, hard to break, and require minimal tuning.

elements.title: K-Means Clustering
elements.content_inline:
K-Means Clustering

K-Means is an unsupervised algorithm that groups n data points into k clusters. The algorithm:

  1. Initialize k centroids randomly
  2. Assign each point to the nearest centroid
  3. Recompute centroids as the mean of assigned points
  4. Repeat steps 2-3 until convergence

K-Means minimizes within-cluster sum of squares (inertia). Choosing k: use the elbow method (plot inertia vs k, pick the "bend") or silhouette score.

Limitations: assumes spherical clusters of similar size, sensitive to initialization (use k-means++ for better starts), doesn't handle non-convex shapes. For complex cluster shapes, consider DBSCAN.

elements.title: Classify or Cluster?
K-Means Interactive Visualization
elements.content_inline:
K-Means Interactive Visualization

Explore how the K-Means algorithm works by interacting with a 2D scatter plot.

Controls

  • Click on the canvas to place data points
  • Set K: choose the number of clusters (2-6)
  • Initialize: randomly place K centroids (shown as larger colored circles)
  • Step: run one iteration — assign points to nearest centroid, then recompute centroids
  • Run to convergence: auto-iterate until centroids stop moving

Experiments to Try

  1. Place 3 well-separated clusters and run K-Means with K=3. Does it find them?
  2. Try K=2 on the same 3-cluster data. What happens?
  3. Place points in a ring shape and try K=2. Does K-Means handle non-convex shapes?
  4. Run the algorithm multiple times with the same data. Do you always get the same result?

This demonstrates why K-Means is sensitive to initialization and why k-means++ uses smarter initial centroid placement.

chapters.title: Neural Networks

elements.title: Neural Network Architecture
elements.content_inline:
Neural Network Architecture

A neural network is a composition of linear transformations and non-linear activations:

layer(x) = activation(Wx + b)

Common activations: ReLU (max(0, x)) for hidden layers, softmax for multi-class output, sigmoid for binary output.

Architecture choices:

  • Width: neurons per layer (more = more capacity)
  • Depth: number of layers (deeper = more abstract features)
  • Skip connections: allow gradients to flow through deep networks (ResNet)

The universal approximation theorem says a single hidden layer with enough neurons can approximate any continuous function — but deeper networks learn more efficiently in practice.

elements.title: Backpropagation
elements.content_inline:
Backpropagation

Backpropagation computes gradients of the loss with respect to every parameter in the network, using the chain rule of calculus applied layer by layer from output to input.

For a simple two-layer network with loss L:

∂L/∂W₂ = ∂L/∂ŷ · ∂ŷ/∂z₂ · ∂z₂/∂W₂
∂L/∂W₁ = ∂L/∂ŷ · ∂ŷ/∂z₂ · ∂z₂/∂a₁ · ∂a₁/∂z₁ · ∂z₁/∂W₁

Key issues and solutions:

  • Vanishing gradients: use ReLU instead of sigmoid/tanh in hidden layers
  • Exploding gradients: gradient clipping, proper weight initialization (He/Xavier)
  • Slow convergence: adaptive optimizers (Adam) adjust learning rate per parameter

elements.title: Cross-Validation Techniques
elements.content_inline:
Cross-Validation Techniques

Cross-validation estimates how well a model generalizes to unseen data. K-Fold CV:

  1. Split data into k equal folds
  2. Train on k-1 folds, evaluate on the held-out fold
  3. Repeat k times, rotating the held-out fold
  4. Average the scores

Common values: k=5 or k=10. Stratified k-fold preserves class distribution in each fold (important for imbalanced data).

Other variants: Leave-One-Out (k=n, expensive), Repeated k-fold (run k-fold multiple times with different splits), Time-series split (never use future data to predict the past).

elements.title: Block Ciphers & AES
elements.content_inline:
Block Ciphers & AES

A block cipher encrypts fixed-size blocks of plaintext. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is the dominant symmetric cipher, operating on 128-bit blocks with 128, 192, or 256-bit keys.

AES alone only encrypts one block. Modes of operation extend it to arbitrary-length messages:

  • ECB: each block encrypted independently — insecure (reveals patterns)
  • CBC: each block XORed with the previous ciphertext block — requires IV
  • CTR: turns block cipher into stream cipher — parallelizable
  • GCM: CTR mode + authentication tag — the standard choice for authenticated encryption

Always use authenticated encryption (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). Encryption without authentication allows ciphertext manipulation.

elements.title: AES Mode Selection

chapters.title: Public-Key Cryptography
chapters.description: RSA, Diffie-Hellman, elliptic curves

elements.title: RSA Explained
elements.content_inline:
RSA Explained

RSA is based on the difficulty of factoring large semiprimes. Key generation:

  1. Choose two large primes p and q
  2. Compute n = p × q (public modulus)
  3. Compute φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1)
  4. Choose public exponent e (commonly 65537)
  5. Compute private exponent d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n)

Encryption: c = mᵉ mod n. Decryption: m = cᵈ mod n.

RSA is slow (~1000x slower than AES), so in practice it's used to encrypt a symmetric key, which then encrypts the actual data (hybrid encryption). Modern preference is shifting to elliptic curve cryptography for smaller keys and faster operations.

elements.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography
elements.content_inline:
Elliptic Curve Cryptography

ECC achieves equivalent security to RSA with much smaller keys. A 256-bit ECC key ≈ 3072-bit RSA key.

An elliptic curve over a finite field: y² = x³ + ax + b (mod p). The key operation is point multiplication: given a point G and scalar k, compute kG (easy). Given G and kG, finding k is the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (hard).

Common curves:

  • secp256k1: used by Bitcoin
  • Curve25519: designed by Daniel Bernstein, used in X25519 key exchange and Ed25519 signatures
  • P-256 (secp256r1): NIST standard, widely deployed in TLS

elements.title: RSA vs ECC Trade-offs

chapters.title: Hashing & Signatures
chapters.description: SHA-256, BLAKE2, Ed25519, and merkle trees

elements.title: SHA-256 & BLAKE2
elements.content_inline:
SHA-256 & BLAKE2

Cryptographic hash functions map arbitrary data to a fixed-size digest. Properties:

  • Preimage resistance: given h, infeasible to find m such that H(m) = h
  • Second preimage resistance: given m₁, infeasible to find m₂ ≠ m₁ with the same hash
  • Collision resistance: infeasible to find any m₁ ≠ m₂ with the same hash

SHA-256 produces a 256-bit digest. Used in Bitcoin, TLS certificates, and content addressing. Merkle trees chain hashes for efficient verification of large datasets.

BLAKE2 is faster than SHA-256 while maintaining equivalent security. BLAKE3 (used by iroh in this app) is even faster, with built-in parallelism and a tree structure.

elements.title: Digital Signatures with Ed25519
elements.content_inline:
Digital Signatures with Ed25519

A digital signature proves that a message was created by the holder of a specific private key, without revealing the key itself.

Ed25519 uses the Edwards curve Curve25519. It produces 64-byte signatures with 32-byte keys. Advantages:

  • Fast: ~70,000 signatures/second on commodity hardware
  • Deterministic: same message + key always produces the same signature (no random nonce needed)
  • Resistant to side-channel attacks by design

Verification: given (message, signature, public_key), anyone can check validity without the private key. This is the foundation of blockchain transactions, code signing, and certificate chains.

chapters.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs
chapters.description: ZK-SNARKs, ZK-STARKs, and privacy applications

elements.title: Introduction to ZK Proofs
elements.content_inline:
Introduction to ZK Proofs

A zero-knowledge proof lets you prove you know something without revealing what you know. Three properties:

  • Completeness: if the statement is true, the verifier will be convinced
  • Soundness: if the statement is false, the prover can't convince the verifier (except with negligible probability)
  • Zero-knowledge: the verifier learns nothing beyond the truth of the statement

ZK-SNARKs: Succinct Non-interactive Arguments of Knowledge. Proofs are tiny (~200 bytes) and fast to verify, but require a trusted setup. Used in Zcash.

ZK-STARKs: Scalable Transparent Arguments of Knowledge. No trusted setup, quantum-resistant, but larger proofs. Used in StarkNet.

Applications: private transactions, identity verification (prove you're over 18 without revealing your age), verifiable computation.

elements.title: ZK Proof Interactive Demo
elements.content_inline:
ZK Proof Interactive Demo

Experience the magic of zero-knowledge proofs through a classic example: the "Ali Baba Cave" protocol.

The Setup

There is a circular cave with a locked door in the middle. You (the prover) claim to know the secret word that opens the door. I (the verifier) want proof without learning the secret.

The Protocol

  1. You enter the cave and choose path A or path B (I don't watch)
  2. I shout which path I want you to come out from
  3. If you know the secret, you can always come out the correct path (through the door if needed)
  4. If you DON'T know the secret, you can only come out the correct path 50% of the time
  5. We repeat N times — after 20 rounds, I'm 99.9999% confident you know the secret

Interact

Click "Enter Cave" to start a round. Choose a path. The verifier will challenge you. Try both scenarios: knowing the secret and not knowing it. Observe how the probability of faking it drops exponentially with each round.

This is exactly the structure of real ZK-SNARKs and ZK-STARKs, just with mathematical commitments instead of cave paths.

elements.title: Planning User Interviews
elements.content_inline:
Planning User Interviews

User interviews are semi-structured conversations that uncover needs, behaviors, and pain points. Planning steps:

  1. Define research questions: what do you want to learn? (not what to ask — those are different)
  2. Recruit participants: 5-8 users per segment is usually sufficient for qualitative insights
  3. Write an interview guide: open-ended questions, ordered from broad to specific
  4. Prepare logistics: recording consent, note-taker, 30-60 min sessions

Key techniques: ask "why" and "how" (not just "what"), follow up on unexpected answers, avoid leading questions ("Don't you think X is confusing?" → "How did you find X?").

elements.title: Creating Personas
elements.content_inline:
Creating Personas

Personas are fictional archetypes that represent key user segments. A good persona includes:

  • Demographics: name, age, role, tech comfort level
  • Goals: what they're trying to achieve
  • Frustrations: current pain points
  • Behaviors: how they currently solve the problem
  • Context: when and where they interact with the product

Personas should be based on research, not assumptions. Aim for 3-5 personas — enough to cover your user base without overwhelming decision-making. The primary persona's needs should drive core design decisions.

elements.title: Card Sorting Workshop
elements.content_inline:
Card Sorting Workshop

Card sorting helps design intuitive information architecture by understanding how users categorize content.

Open sort: participants group cards and name the groups themselves. Reveals their mental model.

Closed sort: participants sort cards into predefined categories. Tests an existing structure.

Process:

  1. Write each content item on a card (30-60 cards is ideal)
  2. Ask 15-20 participants to sort independently
  3. Analyze with a similarity matrix — items frequently grouped together should be near each other in your navigation

Tools: OptimalSort (remote), physical sticky notes (in-person). Results inform your sitemap and navigation labels.

elements.title: Navigation Patterns
elements.content_inline:
Navigation Patterns

Navigation is how users move through your product. Common patterns:

  • Top nav: horizontal bar for primary sections (works for 3-7 items)
  • Side nav: vertical sidebar for apps with many sections (collapsible for mobile)
  • Tabs: for switching between views of the same content
  • Breadcrumbs: show location in hierarchy, allow backtracking
  • Bottom nav (mobile): 3-5 primary destinations

Design principles: keep navigation consistent across pages, highlight the current location, use clear labels (nouns, not verbs), and limit depth to 3 levels. Progressive disclosure: show top-level options first, reveal details on demand.

chapters.title: Wireframing & Prototyping

elements.title: Low-Fidelity Wireframes
elements.content_inline:
Low-Fidelity Wireframes

Low-fi wireframes are rough sketches that focus on layout and content hierarchy, deliberately avoiding visual design details.

Tools: pen and paper (fastest), Balsamiq (digital sketchy look), or any whiteboard. The rough aesthetic is intentional — it invites feedback on structure rather than aesthetics.

What to include: content blocks, navigation, key interactions. What to leave out: colors, images, exact copy, fonts.

Process: sketch multiple layout options quickly (5-10 minutes each), get feedback, iterate. Paper wireframes can be tested with users via "paper prototyping" — you play the computer, swapping pages as the user "clicks."

elements.title: Interactive Prototyping
elements.content_inline:
Interactive Prototyping

Interactive prototypes simulate the user experience with clickable screens. They range from simple click-through mockups to high-fidelity simulations.

Tools: Figma (industry standard), Sketch + InVision, or code-based prototypes for complex interactions.

Fidelity levels:

  • Low: linked wireframes, test flow and structure
  • Medium: styled screens, test visual hierarchy and content
  • High: pixel-perfect with animations, test micro-interactions

Prototype only what you need to test. A common mistake is over-investing in prototype fidelity before validating the core concept. Test early and often — 5 users per round, iterate between rounds.

chapters.title: Visual Design Fundamentals
chapters.description: Color, typography, spacing, and design tokens

elements.title: Color Theory for Screens
elements.content_inline:
Color Theory for Screens

Color choices affect usability, accessibility, and emotional response. Key concepts:

  • HSL model: Hue (color), Saturation (intensity), Lightness (brightness) — more intuitive than RGB for design
  • Color harmony: complementary (opposite on wheel), analogous (adjacent), triadic (evenly spaced)
  • 60-30-10 rule: 60% dominant color, 30% secondary, 10% accent

Accessibility requirements (WCAG 2.1): normal text needs 4.5:1 contrast ratio against background, large text needs 3:1. Never use color alone to convey information — add icons or text labels.

Dark mode considerations: don't just invert colors. Use dark gray (#121212) instead of pure black, reduce saturation of colors, and test contrast ratios separately.

elements.title: Typography Best Practices
elements.content_inline:
Typography Best Practices

Typography is the most important design skill — text makes up 80-90% of most interfaces.

Key principles:

  • Type scale: use a consistent ratio (e.g., 1.25 or 1.333) between sizes. Example: 12, 14, 16, 20, 24, 32px
  • Line height: 1.4-1.6 for body text, 1.1-1.3 for headings
  • Line length: 45-75 characters per line for readability
  • Font pairing: combine a serif and sans-serif, or two weights of the same family

System font stacks (system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif) load instantly and match the platform's native feel. For custom fonts, use font-display: swap to avoid invisible text during loading.

elements.title: Propositional Logic Essentials
elements.content_inline:
Propositional Logic Essentials

Propositional logic models statements that are either true or false. We combine propositions using operators:

  • AND (p ∧ q): true when both are true
  • OR (p ∨ q): true when at least one is true
  • NOT (¬p): flips truth value
  • IMPLIES (p → q): false only when p is true and q is false

In engineering, logic appears in query filters, access rules, conditionals, and circuit design. Mastering truth tables helps you reason rigorously about complex conditions.

elements.title: Proof Strategies in Practice
elements.content_inline:
Proof Strategies in Practice

Proofs are structured arguments that establish truth from definitions and prior results. Three common strategies:

  1. Direct proof: assume premises, derive conclusion step by step
  2. Proof by contradiction: assume the opposite, derive an impossibility
  3. Proof by induction: prove base case and inductive step for all n

Example pattern (contradiction): to prove √2 is irrational, assume it is rational, reduce to both numerator and denominator being even, and contradict lowest terms.

elements.title: Set Operations & Counting Rules
elements.content_inline:
Set Operations & Counting Rules

Sets represent collections of distinct elements. Core operations:

  • Union A ∪ B: elements in A or B
  • Intersection A ∩ B: elements in both A and B
  • Difference A \ B: elements in A but not B

Counting basics:

  • Product rule: if task has a choices then b choices, total is a × b
  • Sum rule: mutually exclusive options add
  • Combinations: C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!)

These are foundational for probability, algorithm analysis, and capacity planning.

elements.title: Graph Models for Real Systems
elements.content_inline:
Graph Models for Real Systems

Graphs model relationships: users and follows, services and dependencies, cities and roads. Nodes are entities; edges are relationships.

Practical mappings:

  • Build systems: nodes = tasks, edges = prerequisites (DAG)
  • Social apps: nodes = users, edges = follows/friends
  • Routing: nodes = routers, edges = links with weights

Once modeled as a graph, we can apply BFS/DFS, shortest paths, connectivity checks, and topological sort to answer product and operations questions.

elements.title: Graph Thinking Interactive
elements.content_inline:
Graph Thinking Interactive

Use this exercise to model a real workflow as a graph and reason about bottlenecks.

  1. List 8-10 tasks from a software release pipeline.
  2. Draw dependencies as directed edges.
  3. Find tasks with zero in-degree (can start immediately).
  4. Run a topological ordering and identify the critical path.

Then ask: what single edge removal would increase parallelism the most?

chapters.title: Probability for Engineers
chapters.description: Random variables, expected value, and practical probability

elements.title: Expected Value & Risk
elements.content_inline:
Expected Value & Risk

Expected value is the probability-weighted average outcome:

E[X] = Σ xᵢ P(X = xᵢ)

Engineering uses expected value for trade-off decisions (latency, retries, queue times, failure costs). Two systems can share the same expected value but have different risk profiles due to variance.

When evaluating choices, combine:

  • Expected outcome (average)
  • Variance (how spread outcomes are)
  • Tail risk (rare but expensive failures)

This mindset leads to better reliability and incident-response planning.

elements.title: What a Constitution Actually Does
elements.content_inline:
What a Constitution Actually Does

A constitution is a contract — between a state and its citizens, and between branches of government. It does three things, in roughly this order of importance:

  1. Limits power. It says what the state cannot do to you (usually a bill of rights).
  2. Distributes power. It names the branches of government and says who decides what.
  3. Authorises power. It creates offices (president, parliament, courts) and rules for filling them.

A constitution that is only (3) — an organisation chart — is not a real constitution. Several post-colonial constitutions were drafted well on paper but weak on the first two functions, and the gap shows up decades later as institutional fragility.

elements.title: Separation of Powers in Practice
elements.content_inline:
Separation of Powers in Practice

The classical split — executive, legislature, judiciary — rarely runs clean in practice. What matters is whether each branch can actually check the others. Ask:

  • Executive: Who appoints the cabinet? Who controls the military and police?
  • Legislature: Can it pass laws the executive opposes? Can it remove a minister?
  • Judiciary: Are judges appointed by a single actor? Can their budgets be cut as retaliation?

When one branch can simultaneously appoint, pay, and discipline another, separation is a label, not a safeguard. The design pattern is: every appointing authority needs a confirming authority from a different branch.

elements.title: Federal vs Unitary States
elements.content_inline:
Federal vs Unitary States

A unitary state has one sovereign centre that delegates authority to provinces. A federal state has provinces with their own constitutionally-guaranteed powers that the centre cannot unilaterally take back.

Most "federal" post-colonial states are unitary in disguise — the centre can dissolve a state government, appoint its governor, or withhold its revenue. The test is simple: can the centre legally act against a province without the province's consent? If yes, it is unitary in effect, regardless of what the constitution calls it.

Neither model is inherently better. Federalism handles diverse populations but slows national responses. Unitarism acts quickly but concentrates risk. The choice should match the country's actual social composition, not a template.

chapters.title: Rights You Actually Have
chapters.description: Civil and political rights, press freedom, and judicial independence

elements.title: Civil and Political Rights
elements.content_inline:
Civil and Political Rights

Civil rights protect you from the state: freedom from arbitrary arrest, torture, forced confession, surveillance without warrant. Political rights let you participate in the state: voting, running for office, forming parties, protesting.

The important thing to read in your own bill of rights is the limitation clauses. Most rights are not absolute — they can be restricted under conditions (public order, public health, national security). The question is who decides those conditions apply. A right limited at the discretion of the executive is a much weaker right than one limited only by law, tested in court.

elements.title: Press Freedom Under Pressure
elements.content_inline:
Press Freedom Under Pressure

Press freedom erodes quietly, usually through three vectors:

  • Ownership concentration: a handful of proprietors friendly to power buy up outlets.
  • Criminal defamation + "fake news" laws: vague statutes make reporting legally risky.
  • Advertising pressure: state-owned or state-dependent firms pull ads from critical outlets.

Outright censorship (banning publications) is rare in modern democracies; economic and legal pressure does the same work with plausible deniability. Track who owns what, and which journalists have been charged — not whether the newspaper is officially "free".

elements.title: Judicial Independence
elements.content_inline:
Judicial Independence

Courts are independent when judges can rule against the government and still keep their job, pay, and safety. Three structural tests:

  1. Appointment: who nominates judges, who confirms, and can the executive stack the bench?
  2. Tenure: fixed term or until retirement? Can they be removed without impeachment?
  3. Funding: is the judiciary's budget set by parliament or by the executive, and can it be cut mid-term?

Also watch for "court packing" (expanding bench size to dilute opposition), "court shrinking" (the inverse), and transfer policies that move inconvenient judges to minor benches far from home.

chapters.title: Voting and Elections
chapters.description: Voting systems, election integrity, and public accountability

elements.title: How Voting Systems Differ
elements.content_inline:
How Voting Systems Differ

Three families of systems, with very different outcomes:

  • Plurality / first-past-the-post: most votes wins. Simple; can produce huge parliamentary majorities on 40% vote shares. Common in former British colonies.
  • Proportional representation: seats allocated by vote share. Reflects diversity; usually requires coalitions.
  • Ranked-choice / alternative vote: voters rank candidates; lowest-placed eliminated and votes transferred. Rewards consensus candidates.

A country's voting system shapes its party system more than the other way around. Plurality tends toward two big blocs. PR tends toward many parties and coalition governance. Neither is inherently fairer; both encode a tradeoff between stable governance and accurate representation.

elements.title: Election Integrity: Red Flags
elements.content_inline:
Election Integrity: Red Flags

Election fraud is rarely a single dramatic event. It is usually the accumulation of small, plausibly-deniable irregularities. Watch for:

  • Voter-roll purges close to polling day (especially in opposition strongholds).
  • Polling stations relocated or closed with inadequate notice.
  • Long queues in some areas and none in others.
  • Ballot paper shortages — always at specific precincts.
  • Results delayed in competitive seats, announced quickly in safe ones.
  • Observer access denied at counting centres.

No single flag proves fraud. Multiple flags, clustered in competitive seats, are the signal. Document time, place, and specific irregularity — a diary is worth more than a tweet.

elements.title: Community Organising on a Small Budget
elements.content_inline:
Community Organising on a Small Budget

Most civic impact at the local level happens without institutional money. A practical playbook:

  1. Pick one issue. Not "governance" — "fix the water pump at Ward 7 school".
  2. Find five committed people. They do not have to be rich or well-connected. They have to show up.
  3. Identify the accountable office-holder. Usually one municipal officer, not "the government".
  4. Make one written ask. Specific, dated, signed by named residents.
  5. Document every interaction. Dates, names, what was said.

Most civic campaigns fail because they aim at "the system" instead of one office-holder with one obligation. Shrink the target. Repeat.

elements.title: Political Media Literacy
elements.content_inline:
Political Media Literacy

Not all content in a newspaper is reporting. A practical taxonomy:

  • News report: who, what, when, where; quotes named sources; dated byline.
  • Analysis: same facts, but interprets. Should be labeled as such.
  • Opinion / editorial: argues a position. Labeled.
  • Press release rebroadcast: unlabeled reprinting of corporate or government statements. Often filler; treat with suspicion.
  • Paid content: looks like reporting, isn't. Look for a small "sponsored" or "advertorial" tag.
  • Synthetic/AI-generated content: increasingly common; images and audio can be fabricated convincingly.

The discipline is: before you react to a claim, find its source. If the source is an unnamed "official" or a press release, the claim is weak, regardless of how confidently it is presented.

elements.title: Civic Tech in Practice
elements.content_inline:
Civic Tech in Practice

Civic tech = technology that helps citizens hold institutions accountable. Examples that have worked:

  • Budget trackers that parse government spending data and flag unusual line items.
  • Complaint dashboards that aggregate municipal service failures by ward.
  • Open-data portals that expose public records under Right to Information laws.
  • Election observation tools that let citizen monitors upload real-time incident reports.

Civic tech fails when it is built by engineers who never leave their chairs. It works when built with the communities it serves, starting from their actual questions (usually: "where did my tax money go?" or "why is this service broken?"). Tooling is not the bottleneck; trust is.

chapters.title: Power, Money, and Accountability
chapters.description: Public finance literacy, anti-corruption mechanisms, and the colonial legacy

elements.title: How to Read a National Budget
elements.content_inline:
How to Read a National Budget

National budgets look intimidating but usually have three readable sections:

  1. Revenue: where money comes from. Taxes (income, corporate, VAT), borrowing, grants, resource exports.
  2. Recurrent expenditure: salaries, pensions, interest on debt. Usually 60–80% of the total in developing economies.
  3. Capital expenditure: infrastructure, new schools, hospitals. The "development" portion.

Three questions to ask any budget:

  • What fraction of revenue is consumed by debt interest? (Over 30% is a warning sign.)
  • Is capital expenditure actually executed, or rolled over year after year?
  • Who has discretionary spending authority, and how large is that pool?

Budgets are political documents. The numbers tell you what the government claims it will do; the execution reports tell you what it actually did.

elements.title: Anti-Corruption Mechanisms
elements.content_inline:
Anti-Corruption Mechanisms

Corruption is not a personal failing — it is a systems problem. The mechanisms that reduce it are structural:

  • Asset disclosure for public officials, with independent verification.
  • E-procurement with published tender evaluations.
  • Whistleblower protection that actually protects — legal immunity, not just rhetoric.
  • Right to Information with statutory deadlines and penalties for non-compliance.
  • Independent audit offices whose budget and chief cannot be cut by the executive.
  • Public beneficial-ownership registries so shell companies cannot hide behind opaque structures.

No single mechanism is sufficient. Layered, mutually-reinforcing mechanisms make corruption expensive enough that rational actors often decline to engage in it.

elements.title: The Colonial Legacy
elements.content_inline:
The Colonial Legacy

Many modern institutions in the Global South are direct inheritances from colonial administrative structures — borders drawn for resource extraction, legal codes copied from metropolitan statute books, police forces designed to control rather than serve. This is not blame; it is data.

Three durable legacies:

  • Artificial borders that cut across ethnic and linguistic communities, guaranteeing internal tension.
  • Extractive tax structures that concentrate revenue in the capital, leaving peripheries underfunded.
  • Dual legal systems where imported codes coexist uneasily with customary law.

Recognising this legacy doesn't absolve modern governments; it locates some of the problems they inherited. Reforms that ignore structural inheritance often fail for reasons that look local but are actually historical.

chapters.title: Your First Weeks as a Lead
chapters.description: Building trust and handing off work

elements.title: From Doing to Leading
elements.content_inline:
From Doing to Leading

Most new leads were promoted for being good at the work. The job now is different: your output is the team's output, not your own. The hardest habit to break is reaching for the keyboard when a problem appears.

In the first weeks, aim to listen more than you change:

  • Meet each person one-on-one and ask what is going well, what is frustrating, and what they want to grow into.
  • Learn the team's current commitments before adding new ones.
  • Write down what you hear. Patterns across conversations matter more than any single complaint.

Early credibility comes from small promises kept: following up on what people raised, and saying plainly when you do not yet know.

elements.title: Running One-on-Ones
elements.content_inline:
Running One-on-Ones

A one-on-one is the report's meeting, not a status update. Keep it regular (weekly or every two weeks), protect it from cancellation, and let the report bring the agenda first.

A simple shared document helps: each side adds topics during the week, and decisions and follow-ups are noted under the date.

Useful questions when the agenda is thin:

  • What is taking more energy than it should?
  • What would you change about how the team works?
  • Is there anything I should be doing differently?

Status can travel in writing. Use this time for the things that do not: worries, growth, and feedback in both directions.

elements.title: Delegating Well
elements.content_inline:
Delegating Well

Delegation is handing off an outcome, not a list of steps. A clear handoff covers:

  • What done looks like and why it matters.
  • Constraints: deadline, budget, anything that must not change.
  • Authority: which decisions the person can make alone.
  • Check-ins: how often you will look in, set by their experience with this kind of work.

Match support to experience: someone new to a task needs closer check-ins; someone who has done it many times needs only the goal. Expect results that differ from how you would have done it. If the goal is met, that difference is fine.

chapters.title: Feedback and Coaching
chapters.description: Helping people improve and grow

elements.title: Feedback People Can Use
elements.content_inline:
Feedback People Can Use

Useful feedback names a situation, the behaviour you saw, and its impact. Then it asks a question.

In yesterday's planning meeting (situation), you cut Priya off twice (behaviour), and she stopped contributing (impact). What was going on for you?

Guidelines:

  • Give it soon, while the event is fresh. Give corrective feedback in private.
  • Describe what you observed, not what you assume about motives.
  • Give positive feedback with the same detail, so good work is repeated on purpose.
  • Ask for feedback on yourself regularly. People copy what you model.

elements.title: Coaching with Questions
elements.content_inline:
Coaching with Questions

When someone brings you a problem, the fastest response is the answer. The most useful response is often a question, because people remember solutions they reach themselves.

A simple coaching sequence:

  1. Goal: What would a good outcome look like?
  2. Reality: What has happened so far? What have you tried?
  3. Options: What could you do? What else?
  4. Will: What will you do first, and by when?

Coaching is not always right. When there is real urgency or risk, say what to do and explain later. Mentoring differs again: there you share your own experience, clearly labelled as one view.

chapters.title: Planning the Team's Work

elements.title: Goals and OKRs
elements.content_inline:
Goals and OKRs

Objectives and key results (OKRs) separate where you are going from how you will know you got there.

  • Objective: qualitative and motivating. Make new engineers productive fast.
  • Key results: two to four measurable outcomes. Median time to first merged change falls from 10 days to 3.

Key results measure outcomes, not activity: "launch the onboarding page" is a task; "new hires rate onboarding 4 out of 5 or better" is a result.

Write goals with the team, keep them few, and review progress openly during the period. If a key result turns out to be wrong, change it and say why. That is better than steering by a broken number.

elements.title: Prioritizing
elements.content_inline:
Prioritizing

Every team has more requests than capacity. Prioritizing means choosing what not to do.

Two quick lenses:

  • Impact against effort: do high-impact, low-effort work first; question high-effort, low-impact work hard.
  • Urgent against important: urgent but unimportant work can usually be batched, time-boxed, or handed off.

When new work arrives, make the trade-off visible: "We can take this on if we move the reporting work to next month. Which matters more?" A list of ten top priorities is no priority at all.

elements.title: Meetings That Earn Their Time
elements.content_inline:
Meetings That Earn Their Time

A meeting is expensive: an hour with eight people is a full day of work. Before calling one, check that the goal really needs people talking at the same time. One-way updates usually work better written.

For meetings worth holding:

  • State the purpose and the outcome you need (a decision, a plan, a list of risks) in the invitation.
  • Invite the people needed for that outcome, not everyone who might be interested.
  • When discussion circles, name the decision needed and who will make it.
  • End with written decisions, owners, and dates, and send them out.

chapters.title: Building and Growing the Team
chapters.description: Hiring and reviewing performance

elements.title: Hiring with Structure
elements.content_inline:
Hiring with Structure

Unstructured interviews mostly measure how much the interviewer liked the candidate. Structure makes hiring fairer and more predictive.

  1. Define the role first: the three to five skills that matter most, and what good looks like for each.
  2. Ask every candidate the same core questions, mapped to those skills.
  3. Use behavioural questions: "Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a customer. What did you do?"
  4. Score independently against a written rubric before the panel discusses, so the loudest voice does not set everyone's view.

"Culture fit" judged by gut feel tends to hire people like the interviewers. Ask instead what the candidate would add.

elements.title: Fair Performance Reviews
elements.content_inline:
Fair Performance Reviews

A review should hold no surprises. Anything serious should already have been raised when it happened. The review summarizes a conversation that has been going on all along.

To keep reviews fair:

  • Agree expectations at the start of the period.
  • Keep short notes throughout, to counter recency bias (over-weighting the last few weeks).
  • Compare evidence against the expectations, not people against each other.
  • Calibrate with other managers so the same work earns the same rating across teams.

End every review with agreed next steps: what to keep doing, what to change, and how you will help.

chapters.title: Deciding and Leading Change
chapters.description: Decisions, stakeholders, conflict and change

elements.title: Making Decisions
elements.content_inline:
Making Decisions

Many decisions stall not because they are hard but because nobody knows who decides. Before a contested decision, say who decides, who is consulted, and by when.

Match speed to reversibility:

  • Two-way doors are easy to undo. Decide quickly, with whoever is closest to the work.
  • One-way doors are costly to undo. Slow down, gather input, and write the options down.

Record important decisions briefly: the options, the choice, the reasons, and who decided. Once a decision is made, ask the team to disagree and commit: say your objection, then support the choice fully.

elements.title: Keeping Stakeholders Aligned
elements.content_inline:
Keeping Stakeholders Aligned

Stakeholders are the people affected by your team's work, or able to affect it. List them, note what each needs to know and how often, and choose a channel for each.

A good update leads with what changed, what is at risk, and what you need, before the detail. Bad news travels best early, with options attached: "We will miss 1 March. We can ship the core on time and the export a week later, or ship everything on 8 March."

When stakeholders disagree, do not tell each one what they want to hear. Put the trade-off on the table, name who decides, and write down the result.

elements.title: Working Through Conflict
elements.content_inline:
Working Through Conflict

Disagreement about ideas is healthy. It turns harmful when it becomes personal or blocks work. The key move is separating positions (what people say they want) from interests (why they want it).

Two engineers arguing over a database may share an interest in reliability and differ only on a worry about migration time. Once that is named, options appear.

  • Let people try to resolve it themselves first.
  • Step in when it blocks work or harms people.
  • Ask each side to state the other's view fairly before arguing their own.
  • Close with an agreed next step, and check back later.

elements.title: Leading Change
elements.content_inline:
Leading Change

People rarely resist change itself. They resist uncertainty about what it means for them. Leading change means answering three questions early and often:

  1. Why is this happening, and why now?
  2. What changes for me, and what stays the same?
  3. How do I get help, and how can I shape the details?

Involve the people affected before the plan is final, look for early wins you can show, and change processes and incentives to match, or the old way will quietly return. Treat resistance as information: it usually points to a real cost you have not addressed yet.

elements.title: Welcome · स्वागत है
elements.content_inline:
Welcome · स्वागत है

नमस्ते! यह कोर्स उन लोगों के लिए है जिनकी मातृभाषा हिंदी है और जो अंग्रेज़ी पढ़ना, लिखना और बोलना सीखना चाहते हैं। आपको पहले से अंग्रेज़ी आना ज़रूरी नहीं है।

How this course works · यह कोर्स कैसे चलता है:

  • शुरुआत में समझाने की भाषा ज़्यादातर हिंदी है और उदाहरण अंग्रेज़ी में। हर अध्याय के साथ अंग्रेज़ी बढ़ती जाएगी, और आख़िरी अध्याय लगभग पूरा अंग्रेज़ी में है।
  • नए शब्दों के साथ कोष्ठक में देवनागरी में उच्चारण दिया गया है, जैसे Hello (हेलो)। ध्यान रखें: कुछ अंग्रेज़ी ध्वनियाँ देवनागरी में ठीक-ठीक नहीं लिखी जा सकतीं। ऐसी जगहों पर हम साफ़-साफ़ बताएँगे।
  • हर अध्याय के अंत में एक छोटा quiz (प्रश्नोत्तरी) है। आख़िरी अध्याय में आप अपनी आवाज़ रिकॉर्ड करके किसी tutor या साथी से review करवाएँगे।

Six chapters · छह अध्याय:

  1. Letters and Sounds — अक्षर और ध्वनियाँ
  2. First Words — पहले शब्द
  3. Building Sentences — वाक्य बनाना
  4. Talking About Time — समय और काल
  5. Writing Everyday English — रोज़ की अंग्रेज़ी लिखना
  6. Speaking with Confidence — आत्मविश्वास से बोलना

एक सलाह: रोज़ 20–30 मिनट पढ़ें और हर अंग्रेज़ी उदाहरण को ज़ोर से बोलें। गलतियाँ होंगी, और यही सीखने का तरीका है। Mistakes are how we learn.

elements.title: The 26 Letters · अंग्रेज़ी के 26 अक्षर
elements.content_inline:
The 26 Letters · अंग्रेज़ी के 26 अक्षर

अंग्रेज़ी वर्णमाला (alphabet, उच्चारण: ऐल्फ़बेट) में सिर्फ़ 26 अक्षर हैं। हर अक्षर के दो रूप होते हैं: capital letter (बड़ा अक्षर) और small letter (छोटा अक्षर)।

LetterनामLetterनाम
A aएB bबी
C cसीD dडी
E eईF fएफ़
G gजीH hएच
I iआईJ jजे
K kकेL lएल
M mएमN nएन
O oओP pपी
Q qक्यूR rआर
S sएसT tटी
U uयूV vवी
W wडब्ल्यूX xएक्स
Y yवाईZ zज़ेड

Z को भारत और ब्रिटेन में "ज़ेड" कहते हैं, अमेरिका में "ज़ी"। दोनों सही हैं।

Capital letter कब लिखें?

  • वाक्य के पहले शब्द का पहला अक्षर: My name is Ravi.
  • नाम — लोगों, शहरों, देशों, दिनों और महीनों के: Ravi, Delhi, India, Monday, January
  • "मैं" के लिए I हमेशा capital होता है, वाक्य के बीच में भी: Ravi and I are friends.

Handwriting tips · लिखने के सुझाव:

  • बाएँ से दाएँ लिखें, देवनागरी की तरह। पर ऊपर शिरोरेखा नहीं लगती; हर अक्षर अलग रहता है।
  • चार लाइनों वाली कॉपी में अभ्यास करें: a, c, e, o बीच की जगह में रहते हैं; b, d, h, k, l ऊपर जाते हैं; g, j, p, q, y नीचे जाते हैं।
  • इन जोड़ों में गड़बड़ आम है: b / d, p / q, m / n, u / v। इन्हें रोज़ पाँच-पाँच बार लिखें।
  • पहले पूरी वर्णमाला capital में लिखें, फिर small में, फिर दोनों साथ: Aa Bb Cc।

elements.title: अक्षर और ध्वनि · Letters and Sounds
Letters and Sounds · अक्षर और ध्वनि
elements.content_inline:
Letters and Sounds · अक्षर और ध्वनि अलग हैं

देवनागरी में जो लिखा जाता है, लगभग वही बोला जाता है। अंग्रेज़ी में ऐसा नहीं है: एक ही अक्षर कई तरह से बोला जा सकता है, और कई बार कोई अक्षर बोला ही नहीं जाता। इसलिए हर नया शब्द देखकर और सुनकर सीखें।

Vowels (स्वर अक्षर): a, e, i, o, u, और कभी-कभी y (जैसे my, happy)। बाकी अक्षर consonants (व्यंजन अक्षर) हैं। ध्यान दें: स्वर अक्षर सिर्फ़ 5 हैं, पर अंग्रेज़ी में स्वर ध्वनियाँ लगभग 20 हैं!

एक अक्षर, कई ध्वनियाँ:

LetterExamples (उच्चारण)
acat (कैट), cake (केक), car (कार)
ohot (हॉट), go (गो), do (डू)
ccat (कैट) में "क", city (सिटी) में "स"
ggo (गो) में "ग", page (पेज) में "ज"

Common letter patterns · आम जोड़े:

PatternSoundExamples
shशship (शिप), fish (फ़िश)
chचchair (चेयर), teacher (टीचर)

Silent e (मूक e): शब्द के अंत का e अक्सर खुद नहीं बोला जाता, पर पहले वाले स्वर को उसके "नाम" जैसा बना देता है:

सुझाव: ऐसी dictionary या app इस्तेमाल करें जिसमें शब्द सुनाई दे। नया शब्द लिखते समय उसकी spelling और आवाज़ दोनों याद करें।

elements.title: New Sounds · हिंदी से अलग ध्वनियाँ
elements.content_inline:
New Sounds · हिंदी से अलग ध्वनियाँ

अंग्रेज़ी की कुछ ध्वनियाँ हिंदी में अलग से नहीं होतीं, या हम दो ध्वनियों को एक जैसा बोल देते हैं। देवनागरी इन्हें ठीक-ठीक नहीं लिख सकती, इसलिए यहाँ मुँह, जीभ और होंठ की स्थिति पर ध्यान दें। शीशे के सामने अभ्यास करें।

1. V और W — हिंदी में "व" एक ही ध्वनि है, पर अंग्रेज़ी में ये दो अलग ध्वनियाँ हैं:

  • V: ऊपर के दाँत नीचे के होंठ पर हल्के से रखें और आवाज़ के साथ हवा निकालें — very, van, voice।
  • W: दाँत होंठ को नहीं छूते। होंठ गोल करें, जैसे "ऊ" बोलने वाले हों, फिर खोलें — we, water, window।

अभ्यास: vet / wet, vine / wine, very well।

2. TH — दो ध्वनियाँ। दोनों में जीभ की नोक ऊपर और नीचे के दाँतों के बीच से हल्की-सी बाहर आती है:

  • बिना आवाज़ (voiceless): thin, think, three — "थ" जैसी लगती है, पर थ नहीं है।
  • आवाज़ के साथ (voiced): this, that, mother — "द" जैसी लगती है, पर द नहीं है।

अगर thin को "टिन" बोलेंगे, तो सुनने वाला tin समझ सकता है।

3. Z — नुक़्ते वाला "ज़", "ज" नहीं: zoo (ज़ू), zero (ज़ीरो), busy (बिज़ी), is (इज़)। यह "स" जैसी ध्वनि है, बस गले से आवाज़ के साथ।

4. F — नुक़्ते वाला "फ़": ऊपर के दाँत नीचे के होंठ पर रखें और हवा निकालें। हिंदी का "फ" (दोनों होंठ बंद करके) नहीं: fan (फ़ैन), coffee (कॉफ़ी), life (लाइफ़)। ध्यान दें: fan और pan अलग शब्द हैं।

5. Short and long vowels · छोटे और लंबे स्वर — हिंदी में इ/ई और उ/ऊ का फ़र्क आप पहले से जानते हैं। अंग्रेज़ी में भी यही फ़र्क शब्द बदल देता है:

Short (छोटा)Long (लंबा)
ship (शिप) जहाज़sheep (शीप) भेड़
sit (सिट) बैठनाseat (सीट) सीट
live (लिव) रहनाleave (लीव) छोड़ना
full (फ़ुल) भरा हुआfool (फ़ूल) मूर्ख

ये ध्वनियाँ धीरे-धीरे आती हैं। अध्याय 6 में हम इनका और अभ्यास करेंगे।

elements.title: Greetings and Polite Words · अभिवादन और शिष्टाचार
elements.content_inline:
Greetings and Polite Words · अभिवादन और शिष्टाचार

अंग्रेज़ी में बातचीत लगभग हमेशा किसी अभिवादन से शुरू होती है। ये शब्द रोज़ इस्तेमाल होंगे, इसलिए इन्हें सबसे पहले याद करें।

English (उच्चारण)हिंदीकब बोलें
Hello (हेलो)नमस्तेकिसी से भी, कभी भी
Hi (हाय)नमस्ते (अनौपचारिक)दोस्तों और जान-पहचान वालों से
Good morning (गुड मॉर्निंग)सुप्रभातसुबह, दोपहर 12 बजे से पहले
Good afternoon (गुड आफ़्टरनून)नमस्तेदोपहर 12 से लगभग शाम 5 बजे तक
Good evening (गुड ईवनिंग)नमस्तेशाम को मिलने पर
Good night (गुड नाइट)शुभ रात्रिसिर्फ़ रात को विदा लेते समय या सोने से पहले — मिलने पर नहीं!
Goodbye / Bye (गुडबाय / बाय)फिर मिलेंगेजाते समय

Magic words · जादुई शब्द:

English (उच्चारण)हिंदीExample
Please (प्लीज़)कृपयाCan I have some water, please?
Thank you / Thanks (थैंक यू)धन्यवाद / शुक्रियाजवाब: You're welcome. (योर वेलकम)
Sorry (सॉरी)माफ़ कीजिएगलती होने पर: Sorry, I'm late.
Excuse me (एक्सक्यूज़ मी)सुनिए / ज़रा रास्ता दीजिएध्यान खींचने या रास्ता माँगने के लिए

Thank you में "th" के लिए जीभ दाँतों के बीच रखें; "टैंक यू" न बोलें। देवनागरी का "थैंक" सिर्फ़ अंदाज़ा है।

Sir और Madam: भारत में दफ़्तर, दुकान और स्कूल में "Sir" और "Madam" या "Ma'am" आम हैं और विनम्र माने जाते हैं। कई दूसरे देशों में लोग Mr या Ms के साथ उपनाम (surname) इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जैसे Good morning, Ms Sharma., या सिर्फ़ पहला नाम। दोनों तरीके ठीक हैं; आसपास के लोग कैसे बोलते हैं, सुनकर वैसा ही करें।

A short conversation · छोटी बातचीत:

A: Good morning! How are you? (हाउ आर यू?)

B: I'm fine, thank you. And you?

A: I'm good, thanks.

How are you? अक्सर सिर्फ़ अभिवादन होता है, सवाल नहीं। जवाब छोटा रखें।

elements.title: संख्या, दिन और समय · Numbers, Days and Time
Numbers, Days, Months and Time · संख्याएँ, दिन, महीने, समय
elements.content_inline:
Numbers, Days, Months and Time · संख्याएँ, दिन, महीने, समय

Numbers · संख्याएँ

#English#English
1one (वन)2two (टू)
3three (थ्री)4four (फ़ोर)
5five (फ़ाइव)6six (सिक्स)
7seven (सेवन)8eight (एट)
9nine (नाइन)10ten (टेन)

11–20: eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty। दहाइयाँ: thirty (30), forty (40 — spelling में u नहीं), fifty (50), one hundred (100), one thousand (1000)।

-teen और -ty में फ़र्क: thirTEEN (13) में ज़ोर आख़िर में, THIRty (30) में ज़ोर शुरू में। दाम या फ़ोन नंबर बताते समय यह फ़र्क बहुत ज़रूरी है।

लाख और करोड़: भारत में 1,00,000 लिखते हैं (one lakh)। अंतरराष्ट्रीय अंग्रेज़ी में इसे 100,000 (one hundred thousand) लिखते हैं। 10 लाख = one million, 1 करोड़ = ten million।

Days · दिन (हमेशा capital letter से):

EnglishहिंदीEnglishहिंदी
Monday (मंडे)सोमवारFriday (फ़्राइडे)शुक्रवार
Tuesday (ट्यूज़डे)मंगलवारSaturday (सैटरडे)शनिवार
Wednesday (वेन्ज़डे)बुधवारSunday (संडे)रविवार
Thursday (थर्ज़डे)गुरुवार

Wednesday में पहला d नहीं बोला जाता।

Months · महीने: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December।

Time · समय: What time is it? (व्हॉट टाइम इज़ इट?) — It's seven o'clock.

TimeEnglishहिंदी
7:15seven fifteen / quarter past sevenसवा सात
7:30seven thirty / half past sevenसाढ़े सात
6:45six forty-five / quarter to sevenपौने सात
1:30one thirty / half past oneडेढ़
2:30two thirty / half past twoढाई

a.m. = रात 12 बजे से दोपहर 12 बजे तक; p.m. = दोपहर 12 बजे से रात 12 बजे तक। जैसे 9 a.m. = सुबह 9 बजे, 9 p.m. = रात 9 बजे।

elements.title: Everyday Words · रोज़ के शब्द
elements.content_inline:
Everyday Words · रोज़ के शब्द

आप जितना सोचते हैं, उससे ज़्यादा अंग्रेज़ी पहले से जानते हैं: bus, ticket, station, phone, doctor जैसे शब्द हिंदी में भी रोज़ बोले जाते हैं। नीचे के शब्द रोज़ 10–10 करके याद करें।

Family · परिवार

EnglishहिंदीEnglishहिंदी
mother (मदर)माँfather (फ़ादर)पिता
brother (ब्रदर)भाईsister (सिस्टर)बहन
son (सन)बेटाdaughter (डॉटर)बेटी
husband (हज़्बंड)पतिwife (वाइफ़)पत्नी
grandmotherदादी / नानीgrandfatherदादा / नाना
uncle (अंकल)चाचा, मामा, मौसा, फूफाaunt (आंट)चाची, मामी, मौसी, बुआ

अंग्रेज़ी में चाचा, मामा, मौसा और फूफा सब uncle हैं, और चचेरे-ममेरे भाई-बहन सब cousin। ज़रूरत हो तो साफ़ कहें: my father's brother (चाचा/ताऊ), my mother's sister (मौसी)।

Home and food · घर और खाना

EnglishहिंदीEnglishहिंदी
house / homeघरroomकमरा
kitchen (किचन)रसोईdoor (डोर)दरवाज़ा
window (विंडो)खिड़कीchair (चेयर)कुर्सी
water (वॉटर)पानीrice (राइस)चावल
milkदूधvegetables (वेजिटेबल्स)सब्ज़ियाँ
fruit (फ़्रूट)फलsalt / sugarनमक / चीनी

Work and travel · काम और सफ़र

EnglishहिंदीEnglishहिंदी
officeदफ़्तरjobनौकरी
colleague (कॉलीग)सहकर्मीsalary (सैलरी)तनख़्वाह

Plural · बहुवचन: ज़्यादातर शब्दों में -s जोड़ते हैं: one book, two books। कुछ शब्द अलग हैं: man → men, woman → women (विमिन), child → children।

सुझाव: कार्ड के एक तरफ़ अंग्रेज़ी शब्द और दूसरी तरफ़ हिंदी अर्थ लिखें। घर की चीज़ों पर उनके अंग्रेज़ी नाम की पर्ची चिपकाएँ।

elements.title: Reading Practice · पढ़ने का अभ्यास
elements.content_inline:
Reading Practice · पढ़ने का अभ्यास

1. Signs · सूचना-पट — ये शब्द आपको स्टेशन, दफ़्तर और दुकानों में दिखेंगे:

SignहिंदीSignहिंदी
ENTRY / EXITप्रवेश / निकासOPEN / CLOSEDखुला / बंद
PUSH / PULLधकेलें / खींचेंDANGERख़तरा
NO PARKINGयहाँ गाड़ी खड़ी न करेंWAIT HEREयहाँ इंतज़ार करें

2. A form · फ़ॉर्म

Form fieldहिंदी में मतलब
First name / Surnameपहला नाम / उपनाम
Date of birth (DD/MM/YYYY)जन्म तिथि (दिन/महीना/साल)
Addressपता
Mobile numberमोबाइल नंबर
Signatureहस्ताक्षर

3. A text message · संदेश

Hi Priya, I am running late. The bus is very slow today. I will reach the office at 10:15. Sorry! – Amit

running late = देर हो रही है। सोचिए: अमित को देर क्यों हो रही है? वह कितने बजे पहुँचेगा?

4. A short story · छोटी कहानी — पहले एक बार चुपचाप पढ़ें, फिर ज़ोर से।

Meena lives in Lucknow with her parents. Every morning she wakes up at six o'clock. She drinks a cup of tea and reads the newspaper. Then she takes a bus to her office. She works at a bank near the railway station. In the evening, she walks in the park with her mother. On Sundays, she cooks lunch for the whole family.

WordहिंदीWordहिंदी
livesरहती हैwakes upजागती है
a cup ofएक कपnewspaperअख़बार
takes a busबस से जाती हैnearके पास
cooks lunchदोपहर का खाना बनाती हैwhole familyपूरा परिवार

Questions · प्रश्न (पहले खुद जवाब सोचें):

  1. Where does Meena live?
  2. What does she drink in the morning?
  3. Where does she work?
  4. What does she do on Sundays?

Answers · उत्तर: 1. In Lucknow. 2. Tea. 3. At a bank near the railway station. 4. She cooks lunch for the whole family.

ध्यान दें: she lives, she wakes, she drinks — she/he के साथ क्रिया में -s लगता है। इसके बारे में अध्याय 4 में पढ़ेंगे।

elements.title: Word Order · शब्दों का क्रम
elements.content_inline:
Word Order · शब्दों का क्रम: SOV से SVO

हिंदी में क्रिया (verb) आम तौर पर वाक्य के अंत में आती है: कर्ता + कर्म + क्रिया (Subject–Object–Verb)। अंग्रेज़ी में क्रिया कर्ता के ठीक बाद आती है: Subject + Verb + Object।

हिंदीEnglish
मैं चाय पीता हूँ।I drink tea.
राम किताब पढ़ता है।Ram reads a book.
हम हिंदी बोलते हैं।We speak Hindi.
वह खाना बनाती है।She cooks food.

गलत: I tea drink. ✗ — सही: I drink tea. ✓

am / is / are — हिंदी के "हूँ / है / हैं" के लिए अंग्रेज़ी में am, is, are हैं, और ये भी कर्ता के ठीक बाद आते हैं:

SubjectVerbहिंदी
Iamमैं ... हूँ
He / She / Itisवह / यह ... है
You / We / Theyareतुम / आप / हम / वे ... हो / हैं
हिंदीEnglish
मैं शिक्षक हूँ।I am a teacher.
वह बीमार है।She is ill.
हम तैयार हैं।We are ready.
यह मेरा घर है।This is my house.

हिंदी में "है" अंत में आता है; अंग्रेज़ी में is बीच में। इसे छोड़ें भी नहीं: She ill. ✗ — She is ill. ✓

बोलचाल में छोटे रूप (short forms) आम हैं: I am → I'm, he is → he's, they are → they're।

अभ्यास: शब्दों को सही क्रम में लगाइए — (milk / I / drink) → I drink milk.; (is / my / Asha / sister) → Asha is my sister.

a teacher में a क्यों आया? यह हम दो पाठ बाद पढ़ेंगे।

elements.title: प्रश्न और नहीं · Questions and Negatives
Questions and Negatives · प्रश्न और "नहीं"
elements.content_inline:
Questions and Negatives · प्रश्न और "नहीं"

हिंदी में हाँ/ना वाला प्रश्न बनाने के लिए वाक्य के शुरू में "क्या" जोड़ते हैं, या सिर्फ़ आवाज़ ऊपर उठाते हैं: "तुम चाय पीते हो?" अंग्रेज़ी में शब्दों का क्रम बदलता है।

1. am / is / are वाले वाक्य: इन्हें कर्ता से पहले ले आइए।

  • You are ready. → Are you ready?
  • She is a doctor. → Is she a doctor?

2. बाकी क्रियाएँ: शुरू में do या does (he/she/it के साथ) लगाइए।

  • You drink tea. → Do you drink tea?
  • She lives here. → Does she live here?

does के बाद क्रिया में -s नहीं लगता: Does she lives here? ✗

Negatives · "नहीं" वाले वाक्य: not क्रिया से पहले आता है।

हिंदीEnglish
मैं थका नहीं हूँ।I am not tired.
वह घर पर नहीं है।He is not (isn't) at home.
मैं मांस नहीं खाता।I do not (don't) eat meat.
वह अंग्रेज़ी नहीं बोलती।She does not (doesn't) speak English.

गलत: I not eat meat. ✗ — सही: I don't eat meat. ✓

Question words · प्रश्नवाचक शब्द

EnglishहिंदीEnglishहिंदी
Whatक्याWhoकौन
WhereकहाँWhyक्यों
WhenकबHowकैसे
How muchकितना (दाम, मात्रा)How manyकितने (गिनती)

हिंदी में प्रश्नवाचक शब्द अक्सर बीच में आता है ("तुम कहाँ रहते हो?"); अंग्रेज़ी में शुरू में: question word + do/does/am/is/are + subject + verb।

  • Where do you live? — तुम कहाँ रहते हो?
  • What is your name? — आपका नाम क्या है?
  • Why is he late? — उसे देर क्यों हुई?
  • When does the train leave? — ट्रेन कब छूटती है?

elements.title: A, An, The · आर्टिकल
elements.content_inline:
A, An, The · आर्टिकल

हिंदी में a, an, the जैसे शब्द नहीं होते, इसलिए हिंदी बोलने वाले अक्सर इन्हें छोड़ देते हैं: I am teacher. ✗ अंग्रेज़ी में गिनी जा सकने वाली किसी एक चीज़ (singular countable noun) से पहले लगभग हमेशा कोई शब्द चाहिए — a, an, the, my, this आदि।

A / An — कोई भी एक; पहली बार ज़िक्र; पेशा:

  • I have a phone.
  • She is a nurse. — पेशे के साथ a/an ज़रूरी है।

a या an? यह ध्वनि से तय होता है, अक्षर से नहीं:

an + स्वर ध्वनिa + व्यंजन ध्वनि
an apple, an egga book, a car
an hour (आवर — h नहीं बोलते)a university (यूनिवर्सिटी — "य" से शुरू)
an MBA (एम — स्वर से शुरू)a uniform (यूनिफ़ॉर्म)

The — कोई ख़ास चीज़, जिसे बोलने वाला और सुनने वाला दोनों जानते हैं:

  • I bought a book. The book is very good. — दूसरी बार वही किताब।
  • Please close the door. — इसी कमरे का दरवाज़ा।
  • जो एक ही है: the sun, the moon, the internet
  • नदियाँ और पर्वत-श्रृंखलाएँ: the Ganga, the Himalayas
  • सबसे अच्छा/बड़ा: the best student, the biggest city

कोई article नहीं: आम बात करते समय बहुवचन और न गिने जाने वाले शब्द (I like dogs., Milk is good for health.); नाम (Delhi, India, Ravi); भाषाएँ (I speak Hindi.); खाने के समय (I had lunch.)।

"एक" हमेशा "a" नहीं है: हिंदी के "वह डॉक्टर है" में "एक" नहीं है, फिर भी अंग्रेज़ी में He is a doctor. और जब गिनती ज़रूरी हो, तब "एक" = one: "मेरा एक ही भाई है" → I have only one brother.

✗✓
I am engineer.I am an engineer.
I have car.I have a car.
She is best student.She is the best student.
I went to the Mumbai.I went to Mumbai.

elements.title: In, On, At · प्रीपोज़िशन
elements.content_inline:
In, On, At · प्रीपोज़िशन

हिंदी में "में, पर, से, तक, के साथ" जैसे शब्द संज्ञा के बाद आते हैं: "मेज़ पर", "घर में"। अंग्रेज़ी में ऐसे शब्द (prepositions) संज्ञा से पहले आते हैं।

हिंदीEnglish
मेज़ परon the table
घर मेंin the house
स्टेशन परat the station
दिल्ली सेfrom Delhi
शाम तकuntil the evening
रवि के साथwith Ravi

Place · जगह

  • in — किसी चीज़ के अंदर, या शहर/देश में: in the box, in Mumbai, in India
  • on — किसी सतह पर: on the wall, on the floor; बस/ट्रेन में सवार: on the bus
  • at — किसी ख़ास जगह या बिंदु पर: at the door, at the bus stop, at home, at work

Time · समय

Wordकिसके साथExamples
atघड़ी का समयat 7 o'clock, at noon, at night
onदिन और तारीख़on Monday, on 15 August, on my birthday
inमहीना, साल, दिन का हिस्साin May, in 2025, in the morning, in the evening

याद रखें: at night पर in the morning और in the evening।

हिंदी से आने वाली आम गलतियाँ:

✗✓क्यों
I will go to home.I will go home.home के साथ to नहीं लगता
He is angry on me.He is angry with me."मुझ पर गुस्सा" = angry with
She is married with Raj.She is married to Raj.married के साथ to
I live here since two years.I have lived here for two years.अवधि के लिए for; शुरुआत के लिए since (since 2020)
